Pariksit asks why Rishabhadeva shunned mystic powers; Sukadeva answers that a yogi must never trust the restless mind. Rishabhadeva wanders to South India, his body burns in a bamboo forest fire, and King Arhat later imitates him to found a non-Vedic creed.

children.topic: Why this land is called Bharata-varsa
children.note: The planet, once called Ajanabha-varsa, took the name Bharata-varsa from the reign of Maharaja Bharata. (SB 5.7 3)

children.topic: Every sacrifice offered to Vasudeva alone
children.note: Bharata saw the demigods as limbs of Vasudeva and dedicated all his rituals to Him, which freed him from attachment, lust and greed. (SB 5.7 6)
After ten million years of rule, Bharata divides his wealth among his sons and leaves for Pulaha-ashrama near Hardwar. (SB 5.7 8)

children.topic: A heart melting in ecstatic love
children.note: Bharata's constant service so deepens his love that tears blind him, his hair stands on end, and he forgets even regulative duties. (SB 5.7 12)
Each dawn Bharata praises the Lord in pure goodness who lights the universe, enters it as Supersoul and grants intelligence. (SB 5.7 14)

Bharata rules the earth, now named Bharata-varsa after him, performing sacrifices while offering every result to Vasudeva. After a long reign he leaves his sons the kingdom and retires to Pulaha-ashrama, where solitary worship melts his heart in ecstatic love.

children.topic: 8 · A Description of the Character of Bharata Mahārāja

children.note: Seeing the newborn deer swept down the river, Bharata is moved by compassion and carries it to his ashrama. (SB 5.8 7)

children.topic: Affection for the deer eclipses worship
children.note: Feeding, petting and guarding the fawn, Bharata slowly forgets his spiritual practice and even his worship of the Lord. (SB 5.8 8)

children.topic: Compassion must not ruin one's own path
children.note: A renunciant naturally feels for suffering creatures and may set aside personal interests to protect one who has taken shelter. (SB 5.8 10)

children.topic: Past karma drags a great yogi down
children.note: Sukadeva explains that only unspent fruitive reactions could make a man who left wife and empire fall for a deer. (SB 5.8 26)

children.topic: Thinking of the deer, he becomes one
children.note: Because Bharata's thoughts at death were absorbed in the deer, he takes a deer's body next, though he remembers his past life. (SB 5.8 27)

children.topic: The deer laments his fall from yoga
children.note: In a deer's body Bharata grieves that after leaving home and mastering devotion, his own foolishness undid everything. (SB 5.8 29)

A lion's roar makes a pregnant doe miscarry into the river; Bharata rescues the fawn and grows so attached that his worship lapses. Dying while thinking of the deer, he takes a deer's body but remembers his fall and lives in repentance until death.

children.topic: 9 · The Supreme Character of Jaḍa Bharata
He plays the fool to stay safe
children.note: Remembering his fall, the reborn Bharata acts dull, blind and deaf so nobody engages him, while inwardly fixed on the Lord. (SB 5.9 3)
Degraded men differ from beasts only in leg count; they abuse Jada Bharata, who accepts any food or task without protest. (SB 5.9 9-10)
Set to farm work by his stepbrothers, Jada Bharata gladly eats chaff and burnt scraps without any grudge. (SB 5.9 11)

children.topic: Thieves pick him as a sacrificial animal
children.note: Searching for a man-animal to offer Kali, the dacoits find Jada Bharata guarding a field and bind him joyfully. (SB 5.9 14)
Enraged at the offense against a saint, the goddess leaps from the altar and decapitates the dacoits with their own sword. (SB 5.9 18)

children.topic: The Lord's disc protects the surrendered
children.note: Those who know the soul and wish harm to none are guarded by the Lord and stay fearless even under a raised blade. (SB 5.9 20)

Bharata is reborn as a brahmana who feigns dullness to avoid bad company, so his family calls him Jada Bharata and works him for scraps. Dacoits seize him for a human sacrifice to Kali, but the goddess herself beheads them and saves the devotee.

children.topic: 10 · The Discussion Between Jaḍa Bharata and Mahārāja Rahūgaṇa
Carrying the palanquin while sparing ants
children.note: Jada Bharata checks the ground every few feet to avoid crushing ants, so the palanquin shakes and the king complains. (SB 5.10 2)

children.topic: The body carries the load, not the soul
children.note: Bharata calmly agrees with the king's taunts: since he is spirit, not body, he has neither labored nor grown weary. (SB 5.10 9)

children.topic: Today's king may be tomorrow's servant
children.note: Bharata points out that master and servant are temporary roles set by providence, since all material things begin and end. (SB 5.10 11)
If he truly were a dull madman, Bharata says, the king's punishment would be as useless as beating a dead horse. (SB 5.10 13)

children.topic: The king falls at the sage's feet
children.note: Hearing philosophy that loosens the heart's knot, Rahugana loses his royal conceit and bows his head at Bharata's feet. (SB 5.10 15)

children.topic: Fear only of offending a brahmana
children.note: Rahugana says he fears neither Indra's thunderbolt nor Yamaraja, but he dreads committing an offense against a brahmana. (SB 5.10 17)

King Rahugana's men force Jada Bharata to carry the royal palanquin; his ant-avoiding steps jolt it, and the king mocks him. Bharata replies that he is not the body and no one is truly master or servant. Struck, the king dismounts and begs to learn.

children.topic: Speaking like an expert without experience
children.note: Bharata says the king talks about pains, pleasures and social roles as an inexperienced man would; realized souls do not. (SB 5.11 1)

children.topic: The mind causes bondage and liberation
children.note: Learned scholars agree that one's bodily form, bondage and release are all products of the mind. (SB 5.11 7)
A mind absorbed in sense pleasure brings suffering like a smoky lamp, while a detached mind shines and brings liberation. (SB 5.11 8)
Besides the individual soul, there is Narayana, the self-effulgent Supersoul who pervades creation and shelters all after annihilation. (SB 5.11 13-14)

children.topic: Conquer the mind with the weapon of service
children.note: The uncontrolled mind is the soul's greatest enemy; Bharata tells the king to defeat it by serving the guru's and the Lord's feet. (SB 5.11 17)

Jada Bharata tells Rahugana that talk of master and servant is mere worldly chatter. The mind, chief of the sixteen elements, drives the soul through species and causes both bondage and freedom. He urges the king to conquer it by serving guru and Lord.

children.topic: 12 · Conversation Between Mahārāja Rahūgaṇa and Jaḍa Bharata
Your words are medicine for my fever
children.note: The king confesses the serpent of pride has bitten him and calls Bharata's instructions cooling medicine for his disease. (SB 5.12 2)

children.topic: A cruel king forcing free labor
children.note: Bharata bluntly says forcing unpaid men to carry a palanquin proves cruelty, not the protection of citizens the king imagines. (SB 5.12 7)

children.topic: We are dust and return to dust
children.note: Moving and unmoving beings alike are transformations of earth that rise from it and merge back into it. (SB 5.12 8)
Nondual knowledge is the ultimate truth, realized first as Brahman, then as the Supersoul, and finally as the Supreme Person. (SB 5.12 11)
Neither celibacy, household rules, sannyasa nor fierce austerities reveal the Absolute without the dust of great devotees' feet. (SB 5.12 12)

children.topic: I was Bharata, and fell for a deer
children.note: Jada Bharata reveals his past life as the king who neglected his duties over a fawn and was reborn as a deer. (SB 5.12 14)

Rahugana asks Bharata to explain his teaching simply. Bharata shows the king and his bearers are all transformations of earth, that atoms cannot explain the world, and that the Absolute is known as Brahman, Paramatma and Vasudeva only through devotees' dust.

children.topic: 13 · Further Talks Between King Rahūgaṇa and Jaḍa Bharata
Six plunderers in the forest of the world
children.note: Six powerful robbers waylay the conditioned soul, while family members, like tigers stealing lambs, plunder the merchant's heart. (SB 5.13 2)
Enemies' harsh words sound like owls, fruitless trees fail the hungry traveler, and he chases mirages for water. (SB 5.13 5)

children.topic: Heroes die fighting for borrowed land
children.note: Mighty leaders conquer rivals yet, believing the land theirs, fight and die without ever taking to the spiritual path. (SB 5.13 15)

children.topic: Drop the scepter, take up knowledge
children.note: Bharata advises the king to give up his rod of punishment and sense objects and cut illusion with a knowledge sharpened by devotion. (SB 5.13 20)
Rahugana replies that a human birth outranks even a demigod's, since heaven's comforts leave no room for devotees' company. (SB 5.13 21)
Taught by Bharata, the king sheds bodily identification; anyone sheltered by the Lord's servants can do the same easily. (SB 5.13 25)

Jada Bharata paints material life as a forest where six plunderers rob the merchant-soul, relatives act like jackals, and mirages and thorns torment him. He tells Rahugana to drop his scepter and cut illusion with knowledge; the king sheds bodily identity.

children.topic: 14 · The Material World as the Great Forest of Enjoyment
The senses plunder the merchant's money
children.note: Uncontrolled senses rob the soul of wealth meant for devotion by spending it on seeing, tasting, touching and desiring. (SB 5.14 2)

children.topic: Weeds of family desire grow back
children.note: Like weed seeds that sprout after plowing, the desire for household enjoyment regrows unless completely burned out. (SB 5.14 4)

children.topic: Gold is the yellow stool men chase
children.note: Gold breeds envy and funds illicit sex, gambling, meat and intoxication, luring the passionate like a marsh light mistaken for fire. (SB 5.14 7)

children.topic: The wheel of time is Hari's disc
children.note: The Lord's cakra is time itself, turning from atoms to Brahma's death and spending every life from infancy to old age. (SB 5.14 29)

children.topic: Bharata dropped his empire like stool
children.note: In his prime Bharata abandoned wife, children, friends and a vast kingdom as easily as one discards stool after evacuating. (SB 5.14 43)

children.topic: Hearing of Bharata fulfills every desire
children.note: Those who submissively hear and chant about Bharata gain long life, fame, heaven or liberation, whatever they seek. (SB 5.14 46)

Sukadeva decodes the forest allegory for Pariksit: senses are plunderers, family are tigers, gold is yellow stool, sleep a python, time the Lord's disc. He then praises Bharata, who dropped an envied empire like stool for love of Krishna.

children.topic: 15 · The Glories of the Descendants of King Priyavrata
Sumati mistaken for Buddha in Kali-yuga
children.note: Sukadeva foresees that atheistic people of Kali will imagine Bharata's son Sumati to be Lord Buddha and twist the Vedas to suit them. (SB 5.15 1)

children.topic: Gaya's four ways of caring for citizens
children.note: King Gaya protected property, ensured food, gave gifts, spoke sweetly and instructed his people: the model of royal duty. (SB 5.15 7)

children.topic: When the Lord is pleased, all are pleased
children.note: Satisfying the Supreme Lord satisfies every being from Brahma to grass, and He Himself told Gaya He was fully pleased. (SB 5.15 13)
A famous verse compares King Viraja adorning his dynasty to Vishnu blessing and decorating the demigods. (SB 5.15 16)

Sukadeva traces Bharata's line: Sumati, whom Kali-age atheists will mistake for Buddha, down to saintly King Gaya, who fed, gifted, cheered and taught his people so well that Vishnu declared Himself fully pleased. The line ends with jewel-like King Viraja.

children.topic: Seeing the Lord's universal form first
children.note: Pariksit says fixing the mind on the Lord's gross universal form lifts one to pure goodness, from which subtle Vasudeva can be known. (SB 5.16 3)

children.topic: No one can fully describe the universe
children.note: Sukadeva admits the Lord's material energy is limitless and even a lifetime of Brahma could not explain it perfectly. (SB 5.16 4)

children.topic: Bhu-mandala is shaped like a lotus
children.note: The earthly system resembles a lotus whose seven islands form the whorl, with round Jambudvipa in the center. (SB 5.16 5)

children.topic: Golden Sumeru, pericarp of the lotus
children.note: In central Ilavrita stands golden Mount Sumeru, 100,000 yojanas tall, standing as the seed-cup of the lotus-like earth. (SB 5.16 7)

children.topic: A river of jambu fruit juice
children.note: Elephant-sized jambu fruits burst on falling, and their juice becomes the Jambu-nadi that floods Ilavrita. (SB 5.16 19)

children.topic: Residents free of wrinkles and grey hair
children.note: Those who enjoy the products of these rivers know no fatigue, disease, old age or untimely death and live happily. (SB 5.16 25)

Pariksit asks for details of Bhu-mandala. Sukadeva describes the lotus-like earth: Jambudvipa's nine lands and border mountains, golden Sumeru, its four belt mountains with giant trees, lakes of milk and honey, juice rivers, Jambu-nada gold and Brahma's city.

children.topic: 17 · The Descent of the River Ganges

children.note: When Vamana pierced the universal shell with His toenail, the Causal Ocean's water flowed in as the Ganges, pink from His feet. (SB 5.17 1)

children.topic: Dhruva bathes in Ganges water daily
children.note: Knowing the Ganges washes Vishnu's feet, Dhruva accepts it on his head with tears and trembling devotion to this day. (SB 5.17 2)
On Mount Meru the Ganges divides into Sita, Alakananda, Cakshu and Bhadra, each running toward a different ocean. (SB 5.17 5)
Of the nine lands only Bharata-varsa is for fruitive action; the other eight are enjoyed by the pious returning from heaven. (SB 5.17 11)
Shiva is the sole male in Ilavrita, since Durga transforms any man who dares enter into a woman. (SB 5.17 15)

children.topic: Shelter of the Lord conquers the senses
children.note: Shiva prays that unlike us, who feel attraction and hatred, the Lord glances at matter unmoved, so His feet are the way to conquer the senses. (SB 5.17 19)

The Ganges enters the universe through a hole Vamana's toe made, bathes Dhruva and the seven sages, then splits at Meru into four branches flowing to each land. Sukadeva describes the nine varsas and Shiva's prayer to Sankarshana in Ilavrita.

children.topic: 18 · The Prayers Offered to the Lord by the Residents of Jambūdvīpa

children.note: Bhadrashrava marvels that the materialist, knowing death is certain, still hopes to enjoy the wealth of his dead father or son. (SB 5.18 3)
Prahlada begs the thunder-clawed Lord to destroy the demon of fruitive desire in the heart and make devotees fearless. (SB 5.18 8)

children.topic: Prayer for the welfare of the universe
children.note: Prahlada wishes good fortune to all and that envious hearts be pacified through bhakti-yoga and absorption in Krishna. (SB 5.18 9)

children.topic: Never attracted to the prison of family
children.note: Prahlada prays to feel no pull toward home, wife and bank balance, and if attached at all, to be attached to devotees. (SB 5.18 10)

children.topic: All good qualities live in a devotee
children.note: Every demigod's virtue appears in one devoted to Vasudeva, while a non-devotee's qualities have no real worth. (SB 5.18 12)

children.topic: The only true husband and protector
children.note: Lakshmi declares only the Lord, who fears nothing and shelters the fearful, can rightly be called anyone's husband. (SB 5.18 20)
Srila Prabhupada's recorded class: Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 5.18.12. Tap the link to read the transcript and play the audio.
Recorded classes on this chapter, with transcript and audio on vedabase.io. Oldest first.

Rulers of each land pray to a different form of the Lord: Bhadrashrava to Hayagriva, Prahlada to Nrisimha, Lakshmi to Kamadeva, Manu to Matsya, Aryama to Kurma, and Earth to Varaha. Their prayers teach detachment, hearing about Mukunda and universal welfare.

children.topic: 19 · A Description of the Island of Jambūdvīpa
Why Rama appeared as a man
children.note: Rama took human form to kill Ravana and to teach that happiness built around wife and sex breeds misery. (SB 5.19 5)
Hanuman notes that birth, beauty and eloquence earn no friendship with Rama, who accepted uncultured monkeys as friends. (SB 5.19 7)
Narada says a Krishna conscious person afraid to leave a body of stool and urine has wasted his time studying scriptures. (SB 5.19 14)
The gods in heaven marvel at humans in Bharata-varsa who engage in devotion and wish they could be born there themselves. (SB 5.19 21)

children.topic: Short life in Bharata beats Brahmaloka
children.note: A brief human life here can lead to Vaikuntha by surrender, while even ages in Brahmaloka end in rebirth. (SB 5.19 23)

children.topic: No place is worth living without Krishna-katha
children.note: A wise person cares nothing for any planet lacking the river of topics about the Lord, devotees and sankirtana festivals. (SB 5.19 24)

Hanuman worships Rama in Kimpurusha-varsa; Narada worships Nara-Narayana at Badarikashrama. Sukadeva names Bharata-varsa's mountains and rivers and reports the demigods' longing to be born there, since a short human life in India can lead to Vaikuntha.

children.topic: 20 · Studying the Structure of the Universe

children.note: Jambudvipa is ringed by a salt ocean as wide as itself, then by Plakshadvipa, twice as broad, with a golden plaksha tree. (SB 5.20 2)
Plakshadvipa's people take shelter of the sun-god as a reflection of Vishnu, the oldest person who is Veda and religion. (SB 5.20 5)

children.topic: The moon divides the month for food
children.note: Shalmalidvipa's inhabitants honor the moon-god, who splits the month into bright and dark halves to feed gods and forefathers. (SB 5.20 12)

children.topic: King Ghritaprishtha retires to the Lord's feet
children.note: After dividing Krauncadvipa among seven sons, Ghritaprishtha leaves family life, shelters at the Lord's feet and attains perfection. (SB 5.20 20)
By Krishna's will Lokaloka mountain, taller than Dhruvaloka, blocks the rays of every luminary as the border of the three worlds. (SB 5.20 37)
All beings depend on the sun's heat and light, and since it enables seeing, the sun-god is called the master of vision. (SB 5.20 46)

Sukadeva describes the six outer islands and their oceans of sugarcane juice, liquor, ghee, milk, yogurt and sweet water, whose peoples worship the sun, moon, fire, water, air and Brahma. Beyond lie the golden land, Lokaloka mountain and the central sun.

children.topic: Day and night equal at Aries and Libra
children.note: As the sun passes Aries and Libra the days equal the nights; from Taurus days lengthen, then shorten half an hour monthly. (SB 5.21 4)
The sun circles Manasottara mountain past Indra's Devadhani, Yama's Samyamani, Varuna's Nimlocani and the moon's Vibhavari. (SB 5.21 7)
The sun's chariot wheel is the year, with twelve months as spokes, six seasons as rim sections and three caturmasyas as hub. (SB 5.21 13)
Aruna sits before the sun-god steering the horses yet keeps his gaze turned back toward his master. (SB 5.21 16)
The Valikhilya sages, each the size of a thumb, travel before the sun offering eloquent prayers. (SB 5.21 17)

Sukadeva explains the sun's course: equal days at Aries and Libra, lengthening and shortening seasons, its circuit of Manasottara past the cities of Indra, Yama, Varuna and the moon, and its one-wheeled chariot driven by Aruna and praised by tiny Valikhilyas.

children.topic: Ants walking on a potter's wheel
children.note: The zodiac turns with the wheel of time while the sun and planets move like ants across it, so their motions differ. (SB 5.22 2)
Answering the sages' prayers, the Lord appeared as the sun, dividing Himself into twelve parts to create the seasons. (SB 5.22 3)

children.topic: The moon, life of all beings
children.note: Waxing and waning make day and night for gods and forefathers; the moon's cooling nectar nourishes grains and is called Jiva. (SB 5.22 9)
Venus keeps pace with the sun, nullifies planets that obstruct rain, and is therefore auspicious for all beings. (SB 5.22 12)
Saturn takes thirty months to cross one zodiac sign and thirty years for the circle, and is always inauspicious. (SB 5.22 16)
Above Saturn the seven sages, ever wishing the universe well, circumambulate Vishnu's abode, the polestar. (SB 5.22 17)

Pariksit asks how the sun keeps Meru on both its left and right; Sukadeva answers with ants on a potter's wheel. He then lays out the stacked orbits of moon, stars, Venus, Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the seven sages, with the sun as Narayana's form.

children.topic: Dhruva's polestar, pivot of the sky
children.note: By the Lord's will the polestar shines as the central pivot, and invisible time drives all luminaries around it without pause. (SB 5.23 2)
Like bulls yoked to a central pole, the planets and stars keep their own orbits around Dhruva, driven by the wind of time. (SB 5.23 3)

children.topic: The sky as a dolphin, Vasudeva's form
children.note: The machine of stars resembles a shishumara dolphin, considered an incarnation of Krishna on which great yogis meditate. (SB 5.23 4)
Chanting the mantra or simply bowing to the Shishumara form morning, noon and evening destroys recent sins. (SB 5.23 9)

Above the seven sages sits Dhruvaloka, the pivot all stars circle like bulls at a threshing post. Sukadeva maps the sky as the Shishumara dolphin, a visible form of Vasudeva, with planets on its body and Narayana in its heart, and gives a mantra to worship it.

children.topic: Sudarshana chases Rahu from the eclipse
children.note: When Rahu attacks the sun or moon, Vishnu sends His beloved disc, whose heat drives Rahu away; the disturbance is an eclipse. (SB 5.24 3)

children.topic: No sun, no days, no fear of time
children.note: Because sunlight never reaches the lower heavens, time is not counted in days there and the dread born of time is absent. (SB 5.24 11)
Vamana begged three steps from Bali, took the three worlds, then rewarded him with a kingdom richer than Indra's. (SB 5.24 18)

children.topic: One chant, even while stumbling, frees
children.note: Whoever utters the holy name once, even accidentally while hungry or falling, is freed from past reactions that yogis struggle for. (SB 5.24 20)

children.topic: Riches are not the Lord's real mercy
children.note: The Lord did not bless Bali with opulence as mercy, since wealth makes one forget loving service. (SB 5.24 22)
Bali says only his grandfather Prahlada knew his true interest, rejecting both the kingdom and liberation Nrisimha offered. (SB 5.24 25)

Sukadeva places Rahu below the sun, explains eclipses and the Sudarshana disc, then tours the seven subterranean heavens: Bala's women in Atala, Shiva in Vitala, Bali guarded by Vamana in Sutala, Maya in Talatala, and hooded serpents lighting Patala.

children.topic: The universe: a mustard seed on His hood
children.note: Resting on one of Ananta's thousands of hoods, this whole universe looks like a tiny white mustard seed. (SB 5.25 2)
At devastation Ananta grows slightly angry and three-eyed Rudra with trident springs from between His eyebrows to destroy creation. (SB 5.25 3)

children.topic: Hearing of Ananta cuts the heart's knot
children.note: Whoever hears Ananta's glories from a guru in succession and meditates on Him has the age-old knot of desire cut. (SB 5.25 8)
Chanting the Lord's name, even jokingly or by chance, frees the chanter and hearer from sin; who else could one shelter under? (SB 5.25 11)

children.topic: Thousands of tongues cannot describe Him
children.note: The whole universe with its mountains and oceans rests like an atom on His hood; no number of tongues could describe Him. (SB 5.25 12)

Beneath Patala lies Ananta Shesha, the Lord's Sankarshana expansion, who holds the universe like a mustard seed on one hood and releases Rudra at devastation. Sukadeva praises His beauty and says hearing of Him and chanting His name cuts the heart's knot.

children.topic: 26 · A Description of the Hellish Planets
Three grades of hell by knowledge
children.note: Madness earns the lightest hell, knowing sin brings a middle grade, and hardened deliberate sin the severest suffering. (SB 5.26 3)

children.topic: Yamaraja judges under the Lord's rules
children.note: The sun-god's son sits in Pitriloka, has his agents fetch sinners at death, and assigns each an appropriate hell. (SB 5.26 6)
Those who boil animals and birds alive for their tongues are cooked in boiling oil in the hell called Kumbhipaka. (SB 5.26 13)

children.topic: Eating alone makes one a crow
children.note: One who feeds himself without sharing with guests, elders and children becomes a worm devouring worms in Krimibhojana. (SB 5.26 18)

children.topic: Both pious and impious return to earth
children.note: Sinners go to countless hells and the pious to heaven, but both come back to earth once their results are spent. (SB 5.26 37)

children.topic: From universal form to Krishna's form
children.note: A seeker of liberation first steadies the mind on the universal form, then contemplates Krishna's spiritual form and reaches samadhi. (SB 5.26 39)

Pariksit asks why souls land in different conditions. Sukadeva explains the three modes, locates the hells beneath Bhu-mandala near Yamaraja's Pitriloka, and lists twenty-eight hells with their crimes, ending with the universal form as a step toward Krishna.
Priyavrata, Rsabhadeva and Bharata Maharaja, then the structure of the universe: planetary systems, the sun, the hellish planets. 26 chapters.

children.topic: 1 · The History of the Life of Ajāmila

children.note: Pariksit objects that repeated sinning and atoning is as useless as an elephant that bathes and then throws dust on itself. (SB 6.1 10)

children.topic: Devotion dispels sin like sun burns fog
children.note: Only pure devotional service uproots sinful tendencies for good, just as sunlight instantly clears away fog. (SB 6.1 15)

children.topic: A liquor pot cannot be rinsed clean
children.note: As a wine jar stays impure however many rivers wash it, non-devotees remain impure despite perfect atonement. (SB 6.1 18)
One who once fully surrenders to Krishna and loves His name and form is freed from sin and never meets Yama's men, even in dreams. (SB 6.1 19)
Seeing fierce men with ropes, terrified Ajamila calls his playing son by name and thus chants Narayana with tears. (SB 6.1 28-29)

children.topic: The silkworm trapped in its own cocoon
children.note: Unable to control mind and senses, the soul spins a web of fruitive acts and, like a silkworm in its cocoon, cannot escape. (SB 6.1 52)

Pariksit asks how to avoid hell; Sukadeva says atonement is like an elephant's bath and only devotion uproots sin. He tells of Ajamila, a brahmana ruined by a prostitute, who at death calls his son Narayana; the Yamadutas explain dharma and his sins.

children.topic: One chant atoned for millions of lives
children.note: The Vishnudutas say Ajamila's helpless cry of Narayana wiped out sins of countless lives; it was offenseless, so he is pure. (SB 6.2 7)

children.topic: The name atones for every heavy sin
children.note: Chanting Vishnu's name is the best atonement for thieves, drunkards, killers of brahmanas, cows or kings, and every other sinner. (SB 6.2 9-10)

children.topic: Even joking or careless chanting counts
children.note: Scholars agree the holy name frees one from endless sin whether chanted indirectly, in jest, as music or neglectfully. (SB 6.2 14)

children.topic: Fire burns grass, the name burns sin
children.note: Whether uttered knowingly or not, the Lord's name reduces all sinful reactions to ashes as fire consumes dry grass. (SB 6.2 18)
Like a medicine that heals a patient unaware of its power, the holy name acts fully even for one ignorant of its value. (SB 6.2 19)

children.topic: If Ajamila went home, why doubt?
children.note: Since Ajamila reached Godhead by a chant aimed at his son, one who chants faithfully and without offense cannot fail. (SB 6.2 49)

The Vishnudutas argue that Ajamila's dying chant of Narayana cleared millions of lives of sin, since the holy name works even chanted unknowingly, and free him. Ajamila repents, practices bhakti at Hardwar, and on seeing them again departs for Vaikuntha.

children.topic: Yamaraja admits he is not supreme
children.note: Yama tells his servants that above him and all demigods is one master who controls the world like a bull led by a nose-rope. (SB 6.3 12)

children.topic: Real dharma comes from the Lord alone
children.note: True religious principles are set by the Supreme Lord and cannot be figured out even by great sages, demigods or Siddhas. (SB 6.3 19)
Yama lists Brahma, Narada, Shiva, the Kumaras, Kapila, Manu, Prahlada, Janaka, Bhishma, Bali, Sukadeva and himself as knowers of dharma. (SB 6.3 20-21)
Devotional service beginning with chanting the holy name is the highest religious principle for human society. (SB 6.3 22)

children.topic: Bring me only those who never chant
children.note: Yama orders his men to arrest only those whose tongues never chant Krishna, whose hearts never remember Him, and who never bow. (SB 6.3 29)

children.topic: Sankirtana, most auspicious in the universe
children.note: Sukadeva concludes that chanting uproots even the gravest sins, making the sankirtana movement the most auspicious activity anywhere. (SB 6.3 31)

The baffled Yamadutas ask their master who overruled him. Yamaraja explains that Narayana is supreme, that bhagavata-dharma is known only to twelve mahajanas, and orders them to avoid chanting devotees. He begs the Lord's pardon for Ajamila's arrest.

children.topic: 4 · The Haṁsa-guhya Prayers Offered to the Lord by Prajāpati Dakṣa
Every body is the Lord's temple
children.note: Soma tells the Pracetas the Supersoul lives in every creature, even trees, so no living being should be killed in anger. (SB 6.4 13)
Anger erupts in the body like a bolt from the sky; one who studies the self and subdues it rises above the modes of nature. (SB 6.4 14)
Daksa opens his prayer: the Lord stands beyond maya and experimental knowledge, uncaused, self-sufficient and unseen by conditioned souls. (SB 6.4 23)

children.topic: Krishna is the cause of all causes
children.note: Everything is done by Him, belongs to Him and is offered to Him; He alone existed before all activity and has no other cause. (SB 6.4 30)

children.topic: Theist and atheist point to one truth
children.note: Yogis and Sankhya analysts argue opposite conclusions, yet both approach the same ultimate cause from different angles. (SB 6.4 32)

children.topic: Austerity is My heart, Vedas My body
children.note: The Lord describes Himself: meditation is His heart, mantras His body, sacrifices His limbs and the demigods His very life. (SB 6.4 46)

Sukadeva tells how the angry Pracetas burn the forests until Soma calms them and gives them Marisa; their son Daksa, failing to populate the world, worships the Lord with the Hamsa-guhya prayers and receives Asikni as his wife.

children.topic: 5 · Nārada Muni Cursed by Prajāpati Dakṣa
Narada's riddle of the strange kingdom
children.note: Narada describes a land with one man, a bottomless hole, a two-way river and a razor wheel, hinting that the boys have not grasped the world. (SB 6.5 6-8)

children.topic: The swan that separates spirit from matter
children.note: Scripture is the swan discriminating soul from matter; ignoring its study for temporary work gains nothing. (SB 6.5 18)
Since second birth comes through sastra, its order to end material life is the father's true command the boys must obey. (SB 6.5 20)

children.topic: Narada sings and travels ever onward
children.note: Chanting the Lord's glories with his vina, Narada keeps his mind at Krishna's feet and moves on after liberating the Haryasvas. (SB 6.5 22)

children.topic: Daksa: renunciation must be earned by experience
children.note: Daksa argues that one detaches only after personally tasting the misery of enjoyment; a borrowed renunciation is shallow. (SB 6.5 41)

children.topic: Narada accepts the curse without protest
children.note: Cursed to have no home, Narada replies 'so be it'; a tolerant sadhu could retaliate but chooses mercy instead. (SB 6.5 44)

Daksa's ten thousand Haryasvas, then a thousand Savalasvas, go to beget children but Narada's riddles turn them all to renunciation. Enraged at losing two sets of sons, Daksa curses Narada to wander homeless, and Narada calmly accepts.

children.topic: 6 · The Progeny of the Daughters of Dakṣa

children.note: Daksa distributes his daughters to Yamaraja, Kasyapa, the moon-god and others, seeding the population of the universe. (SB 6.6 2)

children.topic: Garuda and the serpents are born
children.note: Kasyapa's wife Vinata bears Garuda and Aruna; Kadru bears the snakes, and other wives bear birds and locusts. (SB 6.6 21-22)
Daksa's curse leaves the moon wasting away, unable to beget children in his twenty-seven star-wives. (SB 6.6 23)

children.topic: Aditi's sons include the Lord Himself
children.note: Among the twelve Adityas, Narayana descends by plenary expansion as Urukrama, Vamana. (SB 6.6 38-39)
Abandoned by Brhaspati, the demigods take Tvasta's son as their priest though his mother comes from the demons. (SB 6.6 45)

Sukadeva lists Daksa's sixty daughters, married to Dharma, Kasyapa, the moon-god, Angira, Krsasva and Bhuta, and their offspring that fill the three worlds, ending with Tvasta's son Visvarupa, whom the demigods accept as priest.

children.topic: 7 · Indra Offends His Spiritual Master, Bṛhaspati.
Riches that risk a fall are condemned
children.note: Indra repents that pride in a little wealth made him insult his guru; who would want opulence that leads to falldown? (SB 6.7 12)

children.topic: Misleaders board a boat of stone
children.note: Leaders in ignorance and their blind followers sink together like passengers on a stone boat. (SB 6.7 14)

children.topic: Faith in brahmanas, cows and Krishna
children.note: Brahma says those who worship these three are always strong; the demons grew powerful by devotion to Sukracarya. (SB 6.7 24)

children.topic: Guru, father, mother and guest personified
children.note: The acarya embodies the Vedas, a father Brahma, a mother the earth, a guest religion, and every being Lord Vishnu. (SB 6.7 29-30)
Age decides rank in ordinary matters, but a junior advanced in mantras may be honored as priest. (SB 6.7 33)

children.topic: A true brahmana lives by gleaning
children.note: Visvarupa says a real brahmana picks up leftover grains rather than seeking wealth through professional priesthood. (SB 6.7 36)

Puffed up by opulence, Indra fails to greet his guru Brhaspati, who leaves in silence; the demons then defeat the demigods. Brahma explains the offense and sends them to Visvarupa, who agrees to be their priest and gives Indra the Narayana-kavaca.

children.topic: Eight-armed Lord on Garuda, protect me
children.note: The armor opens by invoking the Lord seated on Garuda holding eight weapons, to protect the chanter always. (SB 6.8 12)

children.topic: Matsya in water, Vamana on land
children.note: Each incarnation guards a domain: the fish in water, the dwarf on land and Visvarupa in the sky. (SB 6.8 13)

children.topic: Narayana, save me from false religion
children.note: The prayer asks Narayana, Nara, Dattatreya and Kapila to guard against false dharma, pride, falling from bhakti and karma. (SB 6.8 16)

children.topic: The holy name destroys every fear
children.note: Glorifying the Lord's name and form drives off bad planets, beasts, ghosts, elements and past sins. (SB 6.8 27-28)
The Lord who roared for Prahlada is asked to protect us from poison, weapons, fire and every direction. (SB 6.8 34)

children.topic: Armor against government, thieves and disease
children.note: One who employs this subtle knowledge of Narayana is never troubled by rulers, plunderers, demons or illness. (SB 6.8 37)

Sukadeva explains the Narayana-kavaca that Visvarupa taught Indra: after purifying oneself with mantras, one prays for each incarnation of the Lord to guard every place, hour and danger. The story of Kausika's bones shows its power.

children.topic: Indra divides the sin of brahmana-killing
children.note: After a year of remorse Indra gives quarters of his sin to earth, trees, women and water in exchange for boons. (SB 6.9 6)

children.topic: Vrtra, the demon who covers everything
children.note: Born from Tvasta's fire, the demon grows daily and blankets all planets by his austerity, hence his name. (SB 6.9 18)

children.topic: Holding a dog's tail to cross the sea
children.note: The demigods admit that seeking shelter anywhere but the self-satisfied Lord is like crossing the ocean by a dog's tail. (SB 6.9 22)

children.topic: One drop of nectar and material joy fades
children.note: Those who taste the Lord's glories forget sense pleasure, become friends of all and never return to this world. (SB 6.9 39)

children.topic: A pure devotee asks only for service
children.note: The Lord says nothing is hard to get when He is pleased, yet His devotee requests nothing but devotional service. (SB 6.9 48)

children.topic: Devotee physician never prescribes harmful food
children.note: A pure devotee never encourages a fool in material enjoyment, just as a doctor refuses a patient unhealthy food. (SB 6.9 50)

Indra beheads three-headed Visvarupa for secretly favoring the demons and spreads the sin over earth, trees, women and water. Tvasta's revenge sacrifice produces Vrtrasura, who swallows the demigods' weapons; the Lord sends them to Dadhici for his bones.

children.topic: 10 · The Battle Between the Demigods and Vṛtrāsura
Who would surrender his body, even for Vishnu?
children.note: Dadhici teases that everyone clings to the body above all possessions, so who could surrender it on request? (SB 6.10 4)
One who won't sacrifice his perishable body for religion or others' suffering is pitied even by immovable beings. (SB 6.10 8)

children.topic: Use body and wealth for others
children.note: A body destined for jackals can only do good if engaged with its possessions in helping others. (SB 6.10 10)

children.topic: Dadhici leaves his body in trance
children.note: Controlling senses, life and mind, the sage cuts all bonds and does not even notice his body departing. (SB 6.10 12)

children.topic: Death is certain, so die gloriously
children.note: Vrtrasura tells the fleeing demons that since no one escapes death, one should accept a death that wins fame and heaven. (SB 6.10 32)
Dying absorbed in bhakti-yoga and dying at the front of battle without turning back are both praised by scripture. (SB 6.10 33)

Dadhici jokingly tests the demigods, then gives up his body in trance; Visvakarma forges a thunderbolt from his bones. Indra attacks Vrtrasura on the Narmada, the demons flee, and Vrtrasura rallies them with a speech on glorious death.

children.topic: No glory in killing the fleeing
children.note: Vrtrasura says a true hero never strikes an enemy running in fear; such killing brings neither fame nor heaven. (SB 6.11 4)
Seeing Indra grieving over his wounded elephant, the demon declines to strike again, honoring the code of battle. (SB 6.11 12)

children.topic: Your victory is assured by Vishnu
children.note: Vrtrasura tells Indra the thunderbolt is charged with Vishnu's power and Dadhici's austerity, so he will surely die. (SB 6.11 20)

children.topic: The Lord withholds opulence from devotees
children.note: Those surrendered at His feet are not given wealth, since possessions only breed anxiety, pride and enmity. (SB 6.11 22)

children.topic: Let me serve Your servants again
children.note: Vrtrasura prays to become servant of the Lord's servants, with mind, words and body absorbed in Him. (SB 6.11 24)

children.topic: Longing like a fledgling for its mother
children.note: He yearns for the Lord as chicks await the mother bird, calves the milking hour and a wife her absent husband. (SB 6.11 26)

Vrtrasura rebukes the demigods for attacking fleeing soldiers, fells Airavata with Indra's own club, then spares Indra. Face to face with his brother's killer, he welcomes the thunderbolt and prays only to serve the Lord's servants.

children.topic: Vrtrasura urges Indra to fight on
children.note: When Indra drops his weapon in shame, the demon tells him to lift it and strike rather than mourn his fate. (SB 6.12 6)

children.topic: We all dance as puppets of the Lord
children.note: Like wooden dolls moved by a handler, every being acts by the supreme controller's desire; no one is independent. (SB 6.12 10)

children.topic: Stay equal in victory and defeat
children.note: Since all depends on the Lord's will, one should remain balanced in fame and infamy, gain and loss, life and death. (SB 6.12 14)

children.topic: Battle is a gamble staked on life
children.note: Vrtrasura frames the fight as dice with lives as stakes and arrows as dice; only providence knows the outcome. (SB 6.12 17)

children.topic: Swimming in nectar, who wants ditch water?
children.note: Indra marvels that a devotee immersed in service to Hari has no interest in petty material rewards. (SB 6.12 22)
After his head falls, the demon's spark of life enters the spiritual world as an associate of Sankarsana. (SB 6.12 35)

Vrtrasura loses an arm yet knocks the thunderbolt from Indra's hand, then urges him to pick it up, teaching that victory and defeat rest with the Lord. Indra praises him, is swallowed, cuts his way out and beheads Vrtra, whose soul goes to Sankarsana.

children.topic: 13 · King Indra Afflicted by Sinful Reaction
Narayana's name erases the gravest sins
children.note: The sages assure Indra that chanting the holy name frees even killers of brahmanas, cows or parents. (SB 6.13 8-9)
His guilt appears as an old, bloody, foul-smelling candala woman crying 'wait, wait' after him. (SB 6.13 12-13)

children.topic: A thousand years hidden in a lotus
children.note: Indra lives invisibly in a lotus fiber of the Manasa lake, starving because Agni fears to bring offerings into water. (SB 6.13 15)
Ruling in Indra's absence, Nahusa lusts after Indra's wife and is cursed to become a snake. (SB 6.13 16)

children.topic: Sacrifice dispels sin like sunrise dispels fog
children.note: The asvamedha performed for Narayana wipes out Indra's grave sin instantly. (SB 6.13 19-20)

Everyone rejoices at Vrtra's death except Indra, haunted by the sin of killing a brahmana in the form of a diseased candala woman. He hides a thousand years in a lotus stem at Manasa-sarovara until the sages' horse sacrifice frees him.

children.topic: Few souls are human, fewer are religious
children.note: Among countless living entities, humans are rare, and among them only some follow religious principles. (SB 6.14 3)

children.topic: A devotee of Narayana is rarest of all
children.note: Among millions of liberated souls, a peaceful devotee of Krishna is almost never found. (SB 6.14 5)

children.topic: Sonless opulence is garlands to the hungry
children.note: Citraketu confesses that a kingdom envied by demigods gives him no joy, like sandalwood offered to a starving man. (SB 6.14 25)

children.topic: A son bringing joy and sorrow
children.note: Angira warns that the promised child will bring the king both joy and grief, then departs without waiting. (SB 6.14 29)
Burning with jealousy at the king's neglect, the sonless queens lose their reason and kill the infant. (SB 6.14 43)
Krtadyuti cries that a creator who lets a son die before his father breaks his own laws and shows no mercy. (SB 6.14 54)

Pariksit asks how a demon like Vrtra became a pure devotee. Sukadeva begins the story of King Citraketu, childless despite millions of wives, who receives a son by Angira's blessing; jealous co-wives poison the boy and the whole palace drowns in grief.

children.topic: 15 · The Saints Nārada and Aṅgirā Instruct King Citraketu
What is this dead body to you?
children.note: The sages ask whether the father-son bond existed before, truly exists now or will last, exposing its temporariness. (SB 6.15 2)

children.topic: Souls meet and part like grains of sand
children.note: Waves gather and scatter sand; time likewise brings embodied beings together and separates them. (SB 6.15 3)
Divisions such as nation, family and person are concoctions of those without spiritual knowledge. (SB 6.15 8)
Citraketu realizes exalted devotees travel the world in strange dress just to enlighten attached materialists. (SB 6.15 11)

children.topic: Kingdom and family are a mirage city
children.note: Angira says wife, wealth and ministers are like an imaginary palace in the forest, breeding only fear and grief. (SB 6.15 21-23)

children.topic: Ask who you are and where you go
children.note: Considering whether one is body, mind or soul, and one's origin and destination, frees one from lamentation. (SB 6.15 26)

Narada and Angira find Citraketu collapsed beside his dead son and teach him that bodily relations are as passing as sand grains moved by waves. Recognizing them, the king begs for knowledge; Angira reveals himself and Narada promises a mantra to see the Lord.

children.topic: 16 · King Citraketu Meets the Supreme Lord
The dead son asks: who are my parents?
children.note: Reanimated by Narada, the soul says he has passed through countless births, so these two are not really his parents. (SB 6.16 4)

children.topic: The soul never takes birth or dies
children.note: Beginningless and imperishable, the living being equals the Lord in quality but, being tiny, is deluded into creating bodies. (SB 6.16 9)
The mantra offers obeisance to Vasudeva, Pradyumna, Aniruddha and Sankarsana as Brahman, Paramatma and Bhagavan. (SB 6.16 18-19)

children.topic: The unconquerable Lord conquered by devotees
children.note: Citraketu prays that devotees who want nothing control the Lord because He gives Himself to them. (SB 6.16 34)

children.topic: Once hearing the name frees even a candala
children.note: If merely hearing the holy name purifies the lowest, seeing the Lord face to face surely cleanses everyone. (SB 6.16 44)

children.topic: Sound and Deity are My eternal forms
children.note: The Lord tells Citraketu that omkara and the Deity form are His non-material eternal manifestations. (SB 6.16 51)

Narada makes the dead boy speak: no one is truly his parent, since the soul wanders through bodies. Freed from grief, Citraketu receives a mantra, sees Sankarsana within a week, and hears the Lord explain that He is the source of both soul and matter.

children.topic: Parvati curses Citraketu to a demon birth
children.note: Angered by his mockery of Siva, she sends the king to a sinful demon family so he will not offend saints again. (SB 6.17 15)

children.topic: Citraketu accepts the curse with folded hands
children.note: He calmly agrees, saying happiness and distress come from one's own past deeds, not from the curser. (SB 6.17 17)

children.topic: Curse or blessing, waves in a river
children.note: In the ceaseless flow of this world, heaven, hell, joy and sorrow have no lasting effect. (SB 6.17 20)

children.topic: Heaven, liberation and hell are the same
children.note: Siva says devotees of Narayana fear no condition, wanting only service, so all destinations look alike to them. (SB 6.17 28)

children.topic: Mistaking a garland for a snake
children.note: Judging happiness and distress as good and bad is like fearing a garland or feeling dream emotions. (SB 6.17 30)
Reborn from Tvasta's sacrifice, the devotee king appears as a demon yet keeps full spiritual knowledge. (SB 6.17 38)

Flying over Kailasa, Citraketu laughs at Siva embracing Parvati among sages. Parvati curses him to a demonic birth; he accepts it calmly, and Siva explains that Vaishnavas see heaven, hell and liberation alike. Citraketu is reborn as Vrtrasura.

children.topic: 18 · Diti Vows to Kill King Indra
Kings' bodies end as worms, stool or ashes
children.note: Diti reflects that killing others to protect a body destined for such an end only leads to hell. (SB 6.18 25)

children.topic: A husband represents the Lord for his wife
children.note: Kasyapa says as Vasudeva is worshiped through demigods, a woman worships the Lord through her husband. (SB 6.18 33-34)

children.topic: Kasyapa regrets being captured by his wife
children.note: Realizing attachment let maya in the form of a woman trap him, the sage condemns his own weakness. (SB 6.18 39)

children.topic: One year's vow decides the son's nature
children.note: Kasyapa promises a son who kills Indra if the vow is kept, but a friend of Indra if it is broken. (SB 6.18 45)

children.topic: Indra cuts the embryo into forty-nine
children.note: Entering Diti's womb, Indra slices the golden embryo seven times seven, telling the crying pieces not to weep. (SB 6.18 62)
Indra observes that devotees ask nothing, not even liberation, yet the Lord grants all their wishes. (SB 6.18 74)

After genealogies of the Adityas and Daityas, Sukadeva tells how Diti, grieving her slain sons, wins a boon from Kasyapa for a son to kill Indra and keeps a year-long vow. Indra finds a lapse and cuts her embryo into forty-nine pieces, who live as the Maruts.

children.topic: I ask not for opulence, only obeisance
children.note: The wife prays to the master of Lakshmi and of all yoga, seeking nothing but to bow before Him. (SB 6.19 4)
Vishnu with the goddess of fortune is the source of every blessing, so their joint worship is everyone's duty. (SB 6.19 9)

children.topic: Lakshmi is really the internal energy
children.note: Though she appears as material energy in this world, the goddess of fortune is always the Lord's spiritual potency. (SB 6.19 11)

children.topic: Husband and wife share the result
children.note: Either spouse may perform the vow; because of their bond, both enjoy the fruit. (SB 6.19 18)

children.topic: The vow's fruits for every woman
children.note: An unmarried girl gains a good husband, a widow reaches the spiritual world, the bereaved gain long-lived children. (SB 6.19 26-28)

Sukadeva details the pumsavana vow: a wife, guided by her husband, worships Vishnu and Lakshmi daily for a year with prayers, oblations and prasada, ending with a Karttika fast and a feast. The vow grants children, fortune, a good husband and even liberation.
The history of Ajamila and the holy name, Daksa again, Vrtrasura and King Citraketu, and the rituals for a good child. 19 chapters.

children.topic: 1 · The Supreme Lord Is Equal to Everyone
Read a person by his devotion
children.note: As fire is known to be in wood, one gauges whether someone is godly or demonic by his devotional acts. (SB 7.1 9)

children.topic: Time favors goodness, not the Lord's partiality
children.note: The time factor strengthens sattva so demigods prosper and demons fall; the Lord Himself stays neutral. (SB 7.1 12)

children.topic: Any absorption in the Lord bears fruit
children.note: Whether by hatred, fear, lust, affection or devotion, fixing the mind on Krishna gives the same result. (SB 7.1 26)

children.topic: The worm that became a bee
children.note: As a grassworm turns into a bee by constant fearful thought of it, souls thinking of Krishna regain spiritual bodies. (SB 7.1 28-29)

children.topic: Gopis by lust, Kamsa by fear, Sisupala envy
children.note: Narada lists how different groups attained Krishna's mercy through different intense emotions. (SB 7.1 31)

children.topic: The Kumaras curse Jaya and Vijaya
children.note: Barred at Vaikuntha's gate, the sages send the two doorkeepers to be born among sinful demons. (SB 7.1 38)

Pariksit asks how the impartial Lord can favor the demigods. Sukadeva explains the Lord works through modes and time, then relates Narada's answer to Yudhisthira: Sisupala was the cursed gatekeeper Jaya, who reached Krishna by absorption even in hatred.

children.topic: Cut the root and the branches wither
children.note: Hiranyakasipu reasons that killing Vishnu will dry up the demigods, who live by Him like branches on a root. (SB 7.2 9)

children.topic: Family is travelers at a water stall
children.note: Like strangers sharing a drink and parting, relatives gather briefly and are led away by their own karma. (SB 7.2 21)

children.topic: The soul is deathless; do not lament
children.note: Eternal and distinct from the body, the soul only seems to suffer through misused independence. (SB 7.2 22)

children.topic: Money lost on the street may return
children.note: Yamaraja shows that destiny, not human protection, decides whether one is saved in the jungle or lost at home. (SB 7.2 40)
The boy asks why the queens grieve when the body remains; they never saw the person who actually spoke. (SB 7.2 44)
Weeping for a hundred years will not revive the dead, while the mourners' own lives slip away. (SB 7.2 57)

Enraged by Hiranyaksa's death, Hiranyakasipu vows to behead Vishnu and orders the demons to destroy brahminical culture. To console his grieving mother and nephews, he tells how Yamaraja, as a boy, taught King Suyajna's queens that the soul never dies.
Hiranyakasipu wants invincibility, freedom from aging, all mystic powers and sole rule of the universe. (SB 7.3 1)
He reasons that since Brahma won his seat by austerity, he too can win it over many lifetimes. (SB 7.3 9-10)

children.topic: Brahma finds him inside an anthill
children.note: After years of penance, only bones remain under grass and ants, yet the demon still heats the world. (SB 7.3 15-16)

children.topic: Restored young and golden by Brahma's water
children.note: Sprinkled from the kamandalu, Hiranyakasipu emerges with a thunderbolt-proof body like fire from wood. (SB 7.3 23)

children.topic: Not inside or outside, not day or night
children.note: The demon asks that no dwelling, time, ground, sky, weapon, man or animal may be the cause of his death. (SB 7.3 36)

children.topic: No rival and sole lordship over all
children.note: He also demands to be unkillable by gods, demons or snakes, and to have lasting mystic powers and universal rule. (SB 7.3 37-38)

Hiranyakasipu performs austerities so severe that fire from his head scorches the universe while ants eat his flesh. Brahma revives him and offers a boon; the demon asks never to die indoors or out, day or night, by man, beast, weapon or any created being.

children.topic: All but three demigods worship the demon
children.note: Drunk and red-eyed, he is still served by everyone except Brahma, Siva and Vishnu, by force of his austerity. (SB 7.4 13)

children.topic: Master of the worlds, servant of his senses
children.note: Despite ruling everywhere and enjoying everything, Hiranyakasipu is unsatisfied because his senses rule him. (SB 7.4 19)

children.topic: Envy of Vishnu destroys a civilization
children.note: The Lord warns that hostility to demigods, Vedas, cows, brahmanas and Himself brings swift ruin. (SB 7.4 27)

children.topic: When he harms Prahlada, I will kill him
children.note: The Lord promises to end Hiranyakasipu, despite Brahma's boons, the moment he torments his peaceful son. (SB 7.4 28)
Self-controlled, kind to all, a servant to elders and a father to the poor, Prahlada treats his teachers as the Lord. (SB 7.4 31-32)

children.topic: Prahlada laughs, cries and sings in ecstasy
children.note: Absorbed in Krishna consciousness, the boy shows the symptoms of spiritual love. (SB 7.4 39)

Blessed by Brahma, Hiranyakasipu conquers the three worlds, sits on Indra's throne and takes all sacrificial offerings himself, yet remains a slave of his senses. The demigods pray, and the Lord promises to kill him when he torments his saintly son Prahlada.

children.topic: 5 · Prahlāda Mahārāja, the Saintly Son of Hiraṇyakaśipu
Leave the dark well of household life
children.note: Prahlada says the best lesson is to abandon the waterless well of family attachment and take shelter of the Lord. (SB 7.5 5)

children.topic: Drawn to Vishnu like iron to a magnet
children.note: He tells his teachers his mind moves toward the Lord by His will, so he has no independence in the matter. (SB 7.5 14)

children.topic: The nine processes of devotional service
children.note: Hearing, chanting, remembering, serving, worshiping, praying, serving as servant, friendship and full surrender. (SB 7.5 23-24)
Materialists with uncontrolled senses repeat the same pleasures and slide toward hell, never awakening to Krishna. (SB 7.5 30)

children.topic: Blind leaders lead the blind into a ditch
children.note: Those who follow a guru attached to sense objects miss the goal and stay bound by the ropes of karma. (SB 7.5 31)

children.topic: Dust of a pure devotee's feet
children.note: Only by the mercy of a Vaishnava free of contamination can a materialist become attached to the Lord's feet. (SB 7.5 32)

Asked what he has learned, five-year-old Prahlada tells his father to leave home life for the Lord, then lists the nine limbs of devotion. Hiranyakasipu orders him killed, but tridents, elephants, poison and fire all fail; Prahlada then teaches his classmates.
The rare human body should be used for devotional service from its earliest years, since even a little brings perfection. (SB 7.6 1)

children.topic: Sense pleasure comes on its own
children.note: Bodily happiness arrives automatically by karma just as distress does, so there is no need to strive for it. (SB 7.6 3)

children.topic: Half a lifetime lost to sleep
children.note: Of a hundred years, the uncontrolled sleep away fifty in the darkness of night. (SB 7.6 6)
Thieves, soldiers and merchants risk life itself for wealth, so who in family life can give up the craving for it? (SB 7.6 10)

children.topic: Pleasing the Lord is never difficult
children.note: Narayana is everyone's father, so child or elder, one can always worship Him without obstacle. (SB 7.6 19)

children.topic: Give up enmity, show mercy to all
children.note: Prahlada urges the boys to drop the demonic nature and become well-wishers by sharing devotional service. (SB 7.6 24)

Prahlada teaches his schoolmates to begin devotional service in childhood, since human life is rare and mostly wasted in sleep, play, old age and family ties. Pleasing Narayana is easy for anyone; he says he learned this from Narada, which puzzles the boys.

children.topic: 7 · What Prahlāda Learned in the Womb
Narada vouches for the unborn devotee
children.note: Narada stops Indra from holding Prahlada's mother, declaring the child in her womb a faultless servant of the Lord whom no one can kill. (SB 7.7 10)

children.topic: Body changes six ways, soul never
children.note: Like a tree's fruit, the body is born, grows, changes and dies, but none of these transformations touch the spirit soul within. (SB 7.7 18)

children.topic: Accept a guru and hear, chant, worship
children.note: Prahlada lists the practical steps of bhakti: serve a bona fide guru, offer him everything, and hear and glorify the Lord in devotee company. (SB 7.7 30-31)

children.topic: God sits in every heart, why not worship?
children.note: The Supersoul is everyone's friend and easy to approach, so Prahlada asks why people chase artificial pleasures instead. (SB 7.7 38)

children.topic: Chasing happiness is where distress begins
children.note: Everyone works for happiness, yet one stays happy only while not striving for it; effort for enjoyment brings misery. (SB 7.7 42)

children.topic: Only unalloyed devotion pleases the Lord
children.note: No brahminical status, learning, charity, austerity or vows satisfy God; without sincere devotion all of it is mere show. (SB 7.7 51-52)

Prahlada tells his demon schoolmates how Narada sheltered his pregnant mother after Indra's raid and taught him in the womb. He explains soul versus body and urges them to take up devotion, since wealth and heaven are fleeting.

children.topic: 8 · Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva Slays the King of the Demons
One source of strength for everyone
children.note: Asked where his courage comes from, Prahlada answers that the same Lord who empowers him empowers his father and even Brahma. (SB 7.8 7)

children.topic: The only enemy is an uncontrolled mind
children.note: Prahlada begs his father to see friend and foe equally, since apart from a misguided mind nobody in the world is truly an enemy. (SB 7.8 9)

children.topic: If He is everywhere, show Him here
children.note: Hiranyakasipu mocks Prahlada's all-pervading God and demands to know why He is not visible in the pillar before him. (SB 7.8 12)

children.topic: Neither man nor lion emerges from pillar
children.note: To prove His devotee's words true, the Lord manifests a never-before-seen half-man, half-lion form from the assembly-hall column. (SB 7.8 17)

children.topic: Demon torn apart on the Lord's lap
children.note: Nrsimhadeva, playing with the demon like Garuda with a snake, lays him across His thighs in the doorway and rips him open with His nails. (SB 7.8 29)
Indra confesses the demon had seized the demigods' hearts, and says those who serve the Lord care nothing for opulence or even liberation. (SB 7.8 42)

Hiranyakasipu threatens to kill Prahlada and strikes a pillar, demanding to see God there. Nrsimhadeva bursts out, tears the demon apart on his lap at the doorway, then sits on the throne while Brahma, Siva, Indra and all planetary residents offer prayers.

children.topic: 9 · Prahlāda Pacifies Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva with Prayers
Lord's hand on the boy's head
children.note: Seeing little Prahlada bowing at His feet, Nrsimhadeva lifts him and places His hand on his head, the hand that grants fearlessness. (SB 7.9 5)
A dog-eater who has given everything to the Lord can purify his whole family, while a fully qualified but non-devotee brahmana cannot save himself. (SB 7.9 10)

children.topic: Material happiness is a desert mirage
children.note: Prahlada compares worldly hope to water in a desert; the body is only a breeding ground for disease, yet people keep running after pleasure. (SB 7.9 25)

children.topic: Mercy never shown even to Brahma or Laksmi
children.note: Born among demons, Prahlada marvels that the Lord placed His hand on his head, a favor withheld from Brahma, Siva and the goddess of fortune. (SB 7.9 26)

children.topic: Fearless for himself, anxious for the fools
children.note: Prahlada says he has no fear of material life, absorbed as he is in the Lord; his only worry is for people scheming for family and national happiness. (SB 7.9 43)

children.topic: I refuse to be liberated alone
children.note: Unlike sages who retreat to the Himalayas for their own salvation, Prahlada wants to bring all the suffering souls back to the Lord's feet. (SB 7.9 44)

When Brahma, Siva and even Laksmi dare not approach the furious Nrsimhadeva, the boy Prahlada steps forward. The Lord's touch fills him with ecstasy and he prays on mercy, maya, false happiness and his wish to save the suffering. The Lord is pacified.

children.topic: 10 · Prahlāda, the Best Among Exalted Devotees
A devotee wanting reward is a merchant
children.note: Prahlada says one who trades devotional service for material profit is not a pure devotee but a businessman seeking payment. (SB 7.10 4)

children.topic: You are master, I am servant
children.note: Prahlada defines his whole relationship with the Lord as eternal master and unmotivated servant, wanting nothing else. (SB 7.10 6)

children.topic: The only boon: no material desires
children.note: If the Lord must give something, Prahlada asks that no material wish ever sprout in his heart. (SB 7.10 7)
The Lord tells Prahlada that his father and twenty-one forefathers are purified simply because a devotee took birth in that family. (SB 7.10 18)

children.topic: Blessing demons is like feeding milk to snakes
children.note: The Lord cautions Brahma that granting boons to cruel, envious demons is as dangerous as nourishing a serpent, and forbids it. (SB 7.10 30)

children.topic: Even Krishna's enemies got spiritual bodies
children.note: Because Sisupala and others thought constantly of Krishna, though as an enemy, they attained sarupya liberation like pure devotees. (SB 7.10 40)

Prahlada declines Nrsimhadeva's boons, asking only freedom from desire and pardon for his father. The Lord crowns him king of the demons and warns Brahma against blessing demons. Narada adds Sisupala's salvation and how Krishna helped Siva burn Maya's cities.

children.topic: 11 · The Perfect Society: Four Social Classes
Thirty virtues for every human being
children.note: Narada lists general religious principles for all: truthfulness, mercy, austerity, cleanliness, sense control, nonviolence, charity, scripture study and more. (SB 7.11 8-12)
A brahmana is known by mind and sense control, austerity, cleanliness, forgiveness, knowledge, mercy, truthfulness and full surrender to God. (SB 7.11 21)
Courage in battle, patience, generosity, forgiveness, respect for brahminical culture and cheerful truthfulness define the warrior class. (SB 7.11 22)

children.topic: Serving a devotee husband leads to Vaikuntha
children.note: A wife who follows Laksmi's example in serving her devotee husband goes back to Godhead with him. (SB 7.11 29)
Drops of ghee feed a fire but a flood smothers it; likewise excessive indulgence eventually extinguishes lusty desire. (SB 7.11 33-34)

children.topic: Class is by qualities, not birth
children.note: If someone shows the symptoms of a brahmana, ksatriya, vaisya or sudra, he should be classified accordingly even if born elsewhere. (SB 7.11 35)

Yudhisthira asks Narada about varnasrama-dharma. Narada lists thirty universal virtues, then the duties and qualities of brahmanas, ksatriyas, vaisyas and sudras, emergency livelihoods, the conduct of a chaste wife, and the rule that class follows character.

children.topic: 12 · The Perfect Society: Four Spiritual Classes
The student lives only for the guru
children.note: A brahmacari controls his senses, stays submissive and friendly to the spiritual master, and lives at the gurukula solely for the guru's benefit. (SB 7.12 1)

children.topic: Beg alms, offer all to the teacher
children.note: The student collects alms morning and evening, gives everything to the guru, and eats only when the guru permits. (SB 7.12 5)

children.topic: Woman is fire, man a pot of butter
children.note: Narada warns a man to avoid privacy even with his own daughter, meeting women only for necessary business. (SB 7.12 9)

children.topic: See Vishnu in fire, guru, self and all
children.note: One should realize the Lord as simultaneously inside and outside everything, the full controller in every circumstance. (SB 7.12 15)
The forest dweller avoids cultivated, unripe or fire-cooked grain, living on what ripens naturally in the sun. (SB 7.12 18)

children.topic: When matter returns to matter, spirit remains
children.note: After all material designations merge back into their elements, only the spiritual being remains, one in quality with the Supreme. (SB 7.12 31)

Narada describes the four ashramas: the brahmacari's austere life at the guru's school, strict rules on avoiding women, the forest-dwelling vanaprastha's diet and dress, and how the retired sage merges the body's elements and senses back into their sources.

children.topic: 13 · The Behavior of a Perfect Person
One night per village, then move on
children.note: The renunciant keeps his body barely maintained and travels constantly, never depending on any place or person for bodily needs. (SB 7.13 1)

children.topic: No disciples for gain, no lectures for pay
children.note: A sannyasi must not lure followers with material promises, nor read or lecture merely to earn a livelihood or expand his wealth. (SB 7.13 8)

children.topic: Act like a child, speak like a mute
children.note: The saint hides his greatness from society, presenting himself as restless and dumb even though he is the wisest speaker. (SB 7.13 10)

children.topic: Deer misses the water under the grass
children.note: Like a deer that runs elsewhere for water while a well lies hidden beneath grass, the soul ignores the happiness within and chases the world. (SB 7.13 29)

children.topic: The bee and the python as gurus
children.note: The saint learns from the bee to gather only a little and from the python to stay in one place, satisfied with whatever comes. (SB 7.13 35)

children.topic: Money is honey; its owner can be killed
children.note: From the bumblebee he learned not to hoard wealth, since anyone may kill the collector and take the store away. (SB 7.13 36)

Narada describes the wandering sannyasi who begs, stays one night per village and shuns disciples for profit. Prahlada then meets a fat, dust-covered saint by the Kaveri who lives like a python and learns from bees and pythons to be content with what comes.

children.topic: Work, but give the results to Krishna
children.note: Householders earn their living but should offer the fruits to Vasudeva, learning how to please Him through the company of devotees. (SB 7.14 2)
The wise householder appears devoted to family affairs while inwardly staying free, working only as much as maintaining life requires. (SB 7.14 5)

children.topic: Taking more than you need is theft
children.note: One may own what keeps body and soul together; whoever claims more is a thief punishable by nature's laws. (SB 7.14 8)

children.topic: Treat animals as your own children
children.note: Deer, camels, monkeys, snakes, birds and even flies deserve the care one gives a son; there is little difference between them and children. (SB 7.14 9)

children.topic: Water the root: worship Krishna, serve all
children.note: The universe is a tree rooted in Acyuta, so worshiping Krishna automatically worships every living being. (SB 7.14 36)

children.topic: Preaching brahmanas are honored even by Krishna
children.note: Brahmanas who spread the Lord's glories sanctify the three worlds with their footdust and are worshipable even to Krishna. (SB 7.14 42)

Yudhisthira asks how householders can be liberated. Narada: work but offer results to Krishna, hear from devotees, keep life simple, claim only what you need, feed guests and animals, worship the Supersoul, honor auspicious times, holy places and Vaisnavas.
Giving up envy of all living beings in body, words and mind is declared the topmost religious principle. (SB 7.15 8)

children.topic: Five kinds of irreligion to reject
children.note: Narada names vidharma, para-dharma, abhasa, upadharma and chala-dharma as false religions the wise must abandon. (SB 7.15 12)
Hunger ends with a meal and anger with revenge, but a greedy man stays unsatisfied even after enjoying the whole world. (SB 7.15 20)

children.topic: The guru is the Lord's direct representative
children.note: One who sees the spiritual master as an ordinary man ruins his study; his learning becomes as useless as an elephant's bath. (SB 7.15 26)

children.topic: Body as chariot, senses as horses
children.note: The senses are horses, the mind the reins, intelligence the driver and sense objects the destinations in this classic analogy. (SB 7.15 41)

children.topic: Chanting gives householders the sannyasi's result
children.note: Narada concludes that the holy name is so powerful that even family men easily reach the goal of the renounced order. (SB 7.15 74)

Narada closes his teaching: keep sraddha simple and vegetarian, abandon five false religions, conquer greed and anger, honor the guru, practice yoga, avoid fallen sannyasa, and see the body as a chariot. He shares his past life as the Gandharva Upabarhana.
Prahlada Maharaja and his father Hiranyakasipu, Nrsimhadeva, then the perfect society: varnasrama and civilised human life. 15 chapters.

children.topic: Canto 8 · Withdrawal of the Cosmic Creations
1 · The Manus, Administrators of the Universe
God witnesses even when all is silent
children.note: Manu prays that the Supreme created the world and stays awake as witness when everything sleeps; He knows all though unknown. (SB 8.1 9)

children.topic: Take only your allotment, covet nothing
children.note: Since the Supersoul pervades all beings, Manu teaches one to accept only one's quota and never infringe on others' property. (SB 8.1 10)

children.topic: Follow the Lord's own example of work
children.note: Krishna acts like an ordinary man without craving results, showing the true path of religion; Manu asks everyone to follow Him. (SB 8.1 16)

children.topic: Yajna kills the demons and becomes Indra
children.note: Seeing hungry Raksasas chasing Manu, the Lord as Yajnapati destroys them with the Yamas and takes up the post of heavenly king. (SB 8.1 18)

children.topic: Any book glorifying the Lord is auspicious
children.note: Pariksit notes that whatever narration describes Uttamasloka is pure, glorious and beneficial by that very fact. (SB 8.1 32)

Pariksit asks about the other Manus. Sukadeva describes the first six manvantaras: Svayambhuva Manu's austerities and prayers, the Lord as Yajna rescuing him from demons, then Svarocisa, Uttama and Tamasa Manus, ending with Hari saving the elephant Gajendra.

children.topic: Elephant serving family like an attached man
children.note: Gajendra sprays water over his wives and calves, illusioned by maya just like a man overly devoted to family. (SB 8.2 26)
By fate a strong crocodile grabs Gajendra's leg in the lake, and the mighty elephant struggles with all his power to escape. (SB 8.2 27)
After years of fighting in its own element, the crocodile gains strength while Gajendra's mind, body and senses fade. (SB 8.2 30)

children.topic: Friends and wives cannot save me
children.note: Realizing his relatives are helpless, Gajendra decides to seek shelter of the Supreme Lord, who shelters even the great. (SB 8.2 32)

children.topic: Even death flees from the Lord
children.note: Gajendra surrenders to the mighty, little-known Lord, from whom the serpent of time runs in fear. (SB 8.2 33)

Sukadeva describes Trikuta Mountain in the Milk Ocean and its heavenly lake. The intoxicated elephant king Gajendra bathes there with his herd until a crocodile seizes his leg; after a thousand-year struggle, weakened and abandoned, he resolves to surrender.
Gajendra opens with obeisances to Vasudeva, the root cause who animates the body and dwells in every heart. (SB 8.3 2)

children.topic: Lord like an actor no one recognizes
children.note: As an audience cannot see through a dancer's costume, neither demigods nor sages can grasp the supreme artist's true features. (SB 8.3 6)

children.topic: An animal has surrendered; You will free me
children.note: Gajendra trusts that the merciful Lord in every heart will release even a beast who has taken shelter of Him. (SB 8.3 17)

children.topic: Not rescue but freedom from ignorance
children.note: Gajendra no longer wishes to keep his elephant body; he asks only to be freed forever from the ignorance that covers him. (SB 8.3 25)

children.topic: Praised no demigod, so only Hari came
children.note: Because Gajendra addressed the supreme authority without naming Brahma, Siva or Indra, none of them appeared, but the Lord did. (SB 8.3 30)

children.topic: Hari cuts the crocodile with His disc
children.note: The Lord descends from Garuda, drags elephant and crocodile from the water and severs the crocodile's jaws as the demigods watch. (SB 8.3 33)

Gajendra recalls a mantra from his past life and prays to the Supreme as the cause of all causes, asking for release from ignorance rather than mere rescue. No demigod responds, but Hari arrives on Garuda and slices the crocodile with His disc.

children.topic: 4 · Gajendra Returns to the Spiritual World
Crocodile was a cursed Gandharva king
children.note: Huhu, turned crocodile by Devala Muni, regains his beautiful form by the Lord's touch and offers prayers. (SB 8.4 3-4)
Touched by the Lord's own hands, Gajendra is freed from all ignorance and receives sarupya-mukti, a body like Vishnu's. (SB 8.4 6)

children.topic: Agastya curses Indradyumna to be an elephant
children.note: Angered that the meditating king failed to welcome him, Agastya condemns him to a dull elephant body in darkness. (SB 8.4 10)

children.topic: Devotee accepts the curse as God's will
children.note: Indradyumna welcomes the curse as the Lord's desire, and his devotion lets him remember how to pray even as an elephant. (SB 8.4 11-12)

children.topic: Rise early, pray like Gajendra, reach Vaikuntha
children.note: The Lord promises an eternal home in the spiritual world to those who wake at night's end and offer Gajendra's prayers. (SB 8.4 25)

The crocodile becomes the Gandharva Huhu, freed from Devala's curse; Gajendra, once King Indradyumna cursed by Agastya, gains a four-armed form and goes to Vaikuntha. The Lord promises liberation to whoever rises early and remembers this pastime and prayer.

children.topic: 5 · The Demigods Appeal to the Lord for Protection
Count the atoms, then count His qualities
children.note: Sukadeva says the Lord's transcendental qualities are as uncountable as the atoms of the universe. (SB 8.5 6)
Weakened by Durvasa's curse and slain by serpent weapons, the demigods cannot be revived and the three worlds sink into poverty. (SB 8.5 15-16)

children.topic: Lord has none to kill or protect
children.note: Brahma explains that God has no favorites or enemies, yet accepts forms in the three modes for creation, maintenance and destruction. (SB 8.5 22)

children.topic: Brahma prays to a Lord never seen
children.note: At Svetadvipa Brahma offers prayers purely from what he has heard in the Vedas, with a fixed mind. (SB 8.5 25)

children.topic: Karmis toil for little, devotees gain beyond hope
children.note: Materialists work hard for unsatisfying results, while devotees achieve more than they expect with little effort. (SB 8.5 47)

children.topic: Water the root and the whole tree lives
children.note: Brahma teaches that serving Vishnu, the Supersoul of all, automatically serves everyone, as watering a root nourishes every branch. (SB 8.5 49)

Sukadeva covers Raivata and Caksusa Manus, then begins the churning story: cursed by Durvasa and beaten by demons, the demigods follow Brahma to Svetadvipa, where he prays to the unseen Lord, calling the universe His body and devotion watering the root.

children.topic: 6 · The Demigods and Demons Declare a Truce
Earth, pot and back to earth
children.note: Brahma says the cosmos comes from, rests in and returns to the Lord, just as a clay pot arises from earth and dissolves back into it. (SB 8.6 10)

children.topic: Bhakti draws the Lord like fire from wood
children.note: As fire comes from wood and milk from a cow, the Lord's favor can be won even in this world through the practice of bhakti-yoga. (SB 8.6 12)

children.topic: Make a truce while time favors the demons
children.note: The Lord advises the weakened demigods to ally with the asuras until their own fortunes recover. (SB 8.6 19)
For an important goal one may even befriend an enemy, as a trapped snake and mouse cooperate until they can escape. (SB 8.6 20)

children.topic: Patience wins; anger loses the goal
children.note: The Lord instructs the demigods to agree to whatever the demons ask, since a peaceful attitude accomplishes what anger cannot. (SB 8.6 24)

children.topic: The Lord's glance revives the crushed
children.note: When Mandara falls and crushes demigods and demons alike, the Lord's mere glance restores them to life without a bruise. (SB 8.6 37)
